content:
I'm pleased to announce an early version of Natural Lean, a library that lets you write Lean definitions, theorems, and proofs in a controlled natural language that looks something like textbook mathematical English. To use the library, you can simply write import Natural at the top of a Lean source file, then write natural-language math freely in the rest of the file. Your text will be translated behind the scenes into native Lean code, which will automatically be checked for correctness in your IDE.

If you're curious, you could look at the file examples/nat_num_game.lean which proves all of the theorems from the Natural Number Game (though often by just appealing to existing lemmas about Nat). The file examples/nat.lean is more substantial: it defines ℕ inductively, defines + and > on ℕ, and proves various theorems about them (associativity, commutativity, trichotomy, ...), all in natural language (and without using Lean's Nat type in any way).

Natural Lean is in an early stage of development and will not be a practical tool for writing many Lean proofs at this time: the grammar and expressiveness of the language are still extremely limited. If you are brave enough to experiment with Natural Lean even in its current primordial state :) then you will certainly encounter bugs, but your feedback is welcome: you can post to Zulip, send me email or open issues in the repository.

Incidentally, Natural Lean is the successor to my earlier standalone natural-language proof assistant Natty, which I worked on for some years before.

I am actively developing this new library and hope to make it useful for real mathematical work in the not-too-distant future. If that happens, it might be a decent target for autoformalizations too.

Broadly speaking, Natural Lean and Lean Verbose have related goals of making Lean code easier to read and write. As I see it, here are some differences:

  1. Natural Lean attempts to go much further in the direction of natural English. The examples from the Lean Verbose paper are nicer to read than native Lean code, but still look something like a Lean proof that has been translated line-for-line into a nicer format. Ideally it will not be easily possible to distinguish between a Natural Lean proof and one that appears in a textbook. For example, Lean Verbose still uses Lean syntax for function application (f x y) and multiplication (a * b * c). In Natural Lean a function application is written with the traditional notation f(x, y), and implicit multiplication is supported so you can write abc for a product.

  2. The steps in a Lean Verbose proof seem to correspond one-for-one with applications of Lean tactics, e.g. in section 3.1 of the Lean Verbose paper there are steps corresponding to applications of change, intro, rcases and so on. It seems that a Lean Verbose author will be aware of these tactics.

    By contrast, in Natural Lean a tactic called default is applied automatically at every step. At the moment it calls grind and aesop which together seem to do pretty well, but it will be configurable so that the developer of any theory in Natural Lean can set it to do anything they want. So ideally an author in Natural Lean shouldn't need to think much about tactics at all - the default tactic should solve many proof steps automatically, and when necessary they can write e.g. by ℕ.is_zero_or_succ, which gives that theorem as an input to the default tactic to help it do its work. The author can also specify an arbitrary Lean tactic when necessary for a given proof step.

  3. As far as I can tell, Lean Verbose is primarily intended for education. I'd like Natural Lean to evolve to the point where it is useful for non-educational purposes, i.e. may be a reasonable alternative to the native Lean syntax for some proofs.

  4. Lean Verbose supports multiple languages. Because Natural Lean is intended to have a grammar that can parse complex mathematical sentences, porting it to other languages will be non-trivial, and is a somewhat more distant goal for this system.
